metadata.scope: e_west_slavia (all 242 baronies across k_bohemia, k_galicia-volhynia, k_moravia, k_poland)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_boleslav.first_mention_attestation: 935 AD (or 929 AD; martyrdom of Duke Wenceslaus I at the gate of the Church of Sts. Cosmas and Damian in Boleslav, recorded in early Wenceslaus legends and Chronica Boemorum; gord founded c. 900 under Spytihněv I).
b_boleslav.eponym_details: Named after Duke Boleslaus I of Bohemia (c. 915–967/972), who fortified the Přemyslid gord with stone walls in the first third of the 10th century. The prefix Stará ('Old') was added by the 14th century to distinguish it from Mladá Boleslav.

morphemes.translation: personal name Boleslav ('greater glory', from Proto-Slavic *bolje 'more' + *slava 'glory')

b_boleslav.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the personal name of Duke Boleslaus I of Bohemia, originally meaning 'Boleslav's castle/gord'. Later distinguished as Stará Boleslav ('Old Boleslav', German Altbunzlau).

older_name_by_867.notes: The Přemyslid gord was founded around 900 AD under Spytihněv I; no pre-867 attestation exists.

b_bezdez.first_mention_attestation: 1264 AD (first written mention of the village; royal castle founded by King Ottokar II in the second half of the 13th century, largely completed by 1279).
b_bezdez.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Bezděd ('without grandfather/ancestor'), not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_bezdez.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Bezděd (early attested form Besdeth), meaning 'Bezděd's (property)'.

b_doudleby.first_mention_attestation: 981 AD (Chronica Boemorum by Cosmas of Prague, written c. 1119–1125, listing Dudlebi among the border strongholds under year 981).

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of the Slavic tribe of Dulebes

b_doudleby.etymology_analysis: Ethnonymic toponym derived from the West Slavic tribe of Dulebes (Czech: Doudlebové), who settled the Malše and upper Vltava basin around 800 AD.

older_name_by_867.notes: Tribal settlement dates archaeologically to c. 800 AD, but the first written mention of Doudleby is under 981 AD.

b_netolice.first_mention_attestation: 981 AD (Chronica Boemorum by Cosmas of Prague, mentioning the border castle of Netolice under the year 981).
b_netolice.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Netol, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_netolice.etymology_analysis: Patronymic settlement name from the Old Czech personal name Netol + -ice, meaning 'village of Netol's people'.

b_rozmberk.first_mention_attestation: 1250 AD (first written mention of Rožmberk Castle, built shortly before 1250 by Vok I of Prčice; town founded in 1262).
b_rozmberk.eponym_details: Named after the heraldic five-petaled rose on the coat of arms of its founder, Vok I of Prčice (House of Rosenberg / Rožmberk), not after a person's given name.
b_rozmberk.etymology_analysis: Czech adaptation (Rožmberk) of Middle High German Rosenberg ('rose mountain/castle'), referencing the five-petaled rose emblem of the Vítkovci/Rosenberg family.

b_krumlov.first_mention_attestation: 1253 AD (first written mention of Krumlov Castle and settlement, founded in the 13th century by the Vítkovci family).
b_krumlov.etymology_analysis: Czech adaptation (Krumlov) of Middle High German Krumme Aue ('crooked meadow'), describing the town's site inside an S-shaped meander of the Vltava River. The modifier Český ('Bohemian') was added in the 15th century.

b_chynov.first_mention_attestation: 981 AD (Chronica Boemorum by Cosmas of Prague, naming the early medieval gord of Chýnov under the year 981).
b_chynov.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Chýna, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_chynov.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Chýna + -ov, meaning 'Chýna's (castle/estate)'.

b_bechyne.first_mention_attestation: c. 1120 AD (Chronica Boemorum by Cosmas of Prague, referencing provincia Bechin / Bechyně gord retrospectively for 993 AD; first contemporary charter mention 1167 AD).
b_bechyne.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Bech, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_bechyne.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Bech + -yně, meaning 'Bech's hill/fortress'.

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeological evidence shows a Slavic gord in the 8th–9th century, but no written attestation exists <= 867 AD.

b_hradec.first_mention_attestation: 1091 AD (recorded in Chronica Boemorum, written 1119–1125; an earlier 1073 charter mentioning castrum Gradec is a 12th-century forgery; city first mentioned 1225).
b_hradec.etymology_analysis: Originally Old Czech Gradec / Hradec ('small castle/fortified settlement', diminutive of hrad). The attribute Králové ('queen's', genitive of králová) was added in the 14th century when it became a dowry town of Bohemian queens.

b_dvur-chvojno.first_mention_attestation: 1270 AD (Latin deed of 27 July 1270 mentioning 'Gottfridus de Curia'; tradition also records Duke Soběslav I visiting Dvůr in 1139).
b_dvur-chvojno.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old Czech dvůr ('princely court/manor') and the older regional/settlement name Chvojno (derived from chvojí, 'conifer boughs/pine forest'), later renamed Dvůr Králové nad Labem ('Queen's Court on the Elbe').

b_jaromer.first_mention_attestation: 1126 AD (first written mention of Jaroměř; early 11th-century Přemyslid gord).
b_jaromer.eponym_details: Named after Duke Jaromír of Bohemia (c. 975–1035), or according to the Chronicle of Dalimil after Bishop Jaromír (c. 1040–1090, son of Bretislav I).
b_jaromer.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Přemyslid personal name Jaromír (initial form Jaromiř), meaning 'Jaromír's (fortress)'.

b_kladzko.first_mention_attestation: 981 AD (Chronica Boemorum by Cosmas of Prague, mentioning castellum Kladsko / Cladzco as belonging to Duke Slavník in 981).

morphemes.translation: log, timber beam (used for fortification palisades or log bridges)

b_kladzko.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Czech kláda ('log/timber beam'), referring to wooden log fortifications or log causeways/bridges at the border stronghold. Adapted into German as Glatz (1291) and Polish as Kłodzko.

b_litomerice.first_mention_attestation: 1057 AD (founding charter of the Litoměřice Chapter by Duke Spytihněv II, the oldest written evidence of the town).
b_litomerice.eponym_details: Derived from the Slavic personal name Ľutomír (or the tribe Litoměřici named after him), not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_litomerice.etymology_analysis: Originally Ľutoměrice, from the personal name Ľutomír + -ice ('settlement of Ľutomír's people'), with u > i shift around 1400.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geographia mentions a Germanic settlement Nomisterium sometimes tentatively localized in the Litoměřice/Lovosice area, but this is not an explicitly attested earlier name of the Slavic town.

b_bilina.first_mention_attestation: 993 AD (privilege of Pope John XV mentioning provincia Belinensis).
b_bilina.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bílina River (earlier Bělá), from Old Czech bielý ('white'), referring either to the sparkling waters of the river or a treeless ('white/bald') clearing.

b_decin.first_mention_attestation: 993 AD (first written mention of the Děčín province, with Děčín as its Přemyslid administrative gord; first mentioned as a town in 1283).
b_decin.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Děk, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_decin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Děk + -ín (with palatalization k > č before í), meaning 'Děk's (castle/ford)'.

b_zitava.first_mention_attestation: 1238 AD (deed of Marienthal Abbey mentioning 'Chastoslaus de Sitavia', i.e., Častolov of Žitava).
b_zitava.etymology_analysis: West Slavic toponym (Upper Sorbian Žitawa, Czech Žitava, Latinized Sitavia, German Zittau) derived from žito ('rye/grain'), referring to fertile grain-growing land.

b_plzen.first_mention_attestation: 976 AD (Chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, recording Duke Boleslaus II's victory 'iuxta Pilisini urbem' at the older Přemyslid gord, today Starý Plzenec).
b_plzen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Czech *Plzeň (attested 976 Pilisini), linked to Proto-Slavic *pьlz- ('slippery/wet terrain'). After King Wenceslaus II founded Nová Plzeň ('New Plzeň') in 1295, the original 10th-century gord became Starý Plzenec ('Old Plzenec').

b_stribro.first_mention_attestation: 1183 AD (deed of Duke Frederick; 16th-century chronicler Wenceslaus Hajek places its founding as a mining settlement in 1131 under Soběslav I).
b_stribro.etymology_analysis: Literally 'silver' in Czech, named for the silver (and later lead) mines established there in the 12th century. The German name Mies derives from the Mže River.

b_primda.first_mention_attestation: 1121 AD (first written mention of Přimda Castle; the town below it is first mentioned in 1331).

morphemes.translation: very faint/dim (or pre-Slavic/Illyrian oronym; German Pfraumberg from Pfrieme 'feather grass')

b_primda.etymology_analysis: Originally the name of the prominent Přimda hill (848 m) and the stream at its foot (possibly from Old Czech prêmda 'very faint', or pre-Slavic), later transferred to the 12th-century border castle and town.

b_domazlice.first_mention_attestation: 993 AD (deed of Duke Boleslaus II mentioning the settlement of Domažlice; royal town founded in 1265).
b_domazlice.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Old Czech personal name Domažil, not a known post-867 historical figure.

morphemes.translation: personal name Domažil (doma 'at home' + žiti 'to live')

b_domazlice.etymology_analysis: Patronymic toponym from the Old Czech personal name Domažil + -ice, meaning 'settlement of Domažil's people'.

b_prachen.first_mention_attestation: 1184 AD (Vítek I of Prčice attested as castellan of Prácheň in 1184; archaeological remains of the Přemyslid gord date from the first half of the 11th century).

morphemes.translation: dust, dry/rotten wood, or rocky promontory

b_prachen.etymology_analysis: Old Czech toponym from the stem prach- / prách- (related to prach 'dust' or práchnivý), designating the fortified promontory above the Otava River that gave its name to the Prácheňsko region.

b_pisek.first_mention_attestation: 1243 AD (dating formula of a charter of King Wenceslaus I; royal town founded c. 1254 by Ottokar II near the earlier gold-panning village Na Písku).

morphemes.translation: sand (specifically the gold-bearing sand of the Otava River)

b_pisek.etymology_analysis: Literally 'sand' in Czech, originally designating the gold-bearing river sand panned by settlers at the Otava River (settlement Na Písku, 'on the sand').

b_praha.first_mention_attestation: 965 AD (travelogue of Ibrahim ibn Yaqub / Abraham ben Jacob c. 965–966, who described 'Frága' as a stone-built trading city; Prague Castle masonry dates to c. 885).

morphemes.translation: threshold/river rapid (or 'to roast/burn', referring to a sun-baked rocky ridge or burned forest clearing)

b_praha.etymology_analysis: Originally Praga (g > h in Czech). Scholars derive it either from Old Czech pražiti ('to roast/burn', referring to the sun-baked shale ridge of Prague Castle or slash-and-burn clearing) or from práh ('threshold/river rapid' across the Vltava).

older_name_by_867.notes: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map mentions a Germanic city Casurgis in the wider region, but it is not an attested earlier name of Prague itself.

b_vysehrad.first_mention_attestation: c. 995 AD (silver denars minted at Vyšehrad under Duke Boleslaus II in the 990s; fort founded in the 10th century).
b_vysehrad.etymology_analysis: Compound of Old Czech vyšší ('upper, higher') + hrad ('castle'), literally 'Upper Castle', referring to its position on a steep rock promontory above the Vltava.

b_beroun.first_mention_attestation: 1265 AD (charter of King Ottokar II mentioning Verona/Beroun; predecessor village Na Brodě 'by the ford' first mentioned in 1088).

morphemes.translation: Verona (Italian city name, adapted as Berona/Beraun/Beroun)

b_beroun.etymology_analysis: Initially attested as Verona (German Bern/Beraun), adapted into Czech as Beroun. Named after the Italian city of Verona (possibly via Italian merchants or German heroic/toponymic transfer).

older_name_by_867.notes: Predecessor settlement Na Brodě was first mentioned in 1088 AD (post-867).

b_melnik.first_mention_attestation: c. 995 AD (denars of Princess Emma, wife of Boleslaus II, bearing the inscription 'EMMA REGINA – CIVITAS MELNIC', minted c. 990s–1005).
b_melnik.etymology_analysis: Originally the Slavic name of the marl/Cretaceous-rock hill above the Elbe-Vltava confluence, derived from Old Czech mělnit ('to crumble').

older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier tribal center of the Pšované (Pšov), but Mělník itself is first attested on late 10th-century coins.

b_slany.first_mention_attestation: 1262 AD (first written mention of Slaný; Benedictine hospital/church of St. Gotthard established in 1136).

morphemes.translation: salty (referring to the salt spring below Slánská hora)

b_slany.etymology_analysis: Literally 'salty' in Czech, named after a natural salt spring at the foot of Slánská hora.

b_milevsko.first_mention_attestation: 1184 AD (first written mention concerning nobleman Jiří of Milevsko; Premonstratensian monastery founded 1187).
b_milevsko.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Milej (via Milejovice > Milevice > Milevsko), not a known post-867 historical figure.

morphemes.translation: toponymic suffix (back-formed from adjective milevský < Milevice)

b_milevsko.etymology_analysis: Originally Milevice (shortened from Milejovice, 'village of Milej's people'), which yielded the adjective milevský and the later neuter form Milevsko.

b_zatec.first_mention_attestation: 1004 AD (Chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, first written mention of the Žatec gord).

natural_proper_name.name: záteč ('narrowed river bend where ice accumulates')

morphemes.translation: flow, current (narrowed river channel where ice jams)

b_zatec.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Czech záteč / zateč, a topographic term for a narrowed river bend where ice accumulates.

b_kadan.first_mention_attestation: 1183 AD (first written mention 'in Kadan'; donated to the Knights Hospitaller in 1186).
b_kadan.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Kadan, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_kadan.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Kadan, meaning 'Kadan's court'.

b_sedlec.first_mention_attestation: 1086 AD (charter of Emperor Henry IV defining the Prague bishopric boundaries, retroactively referencing the 973 foundation of Sedlec / provincia sedlensis).
b_sedlec.etymology_analysis: From Old Czech sedlec ('small settlement/village'), associated with the Slavic tribe of Sedličané (Sedlecko / provincia sedlensis).

b_loket.first_mention_attestation: 1234 AD (first written mention of the town below Loket Castle; royal castle built in the second half of the 12th century).

natural_proper_name.name: Loket ('elbow'-shaped bend of the Ohře River)

morphemes.translation: elbow (referring to the elbow-shaped meander of the Ohře River)

b_loket.etymology_analysis: Literally 'elbow' (German Elbogen, Latin Cubitum), describing the sharp elbow-like bend of the Ohře River surrounding the promontory on three sides.

b_caslav.first_mention_attestation: 1264 AD (foundation of the royal town by King Ottokar II next to the 9th–11th century gord Hrádek; church of St. Michael dates to 1130).
b_caslav.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Čáslav, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_caslav.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Čáslav, meaning 'Čáslav's (settlement/castle)'.

b_vraclav.first_mention_attestation: 1073 AD (first written mention as 'Wratislaw'; early medieval gord built at the turn of the 10th and 11th centuries).
b_vraclav.eponym_details: Derived from the Slavic personal name Vratislav (shortened to Vraclav in the 16th century); not definitively proven to be a specific post-867 duke.
b_vraclav.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the personal name Vratislav ('Vratislav's castle'), contracted to Vraclav from the 16th century.

b_chrudim.first_mention_attestation: 1055 AD (Chronica Boemorum, recording that Duke Bretislav I died at Chrudim in 1055).
b_chrudim.eponym_details: Derived from the unattested Slavic personal name Chrudim, not a known post-867 historical figure.
b_chrudim.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Czech personal name Chrudim, meaning 'Chrudim's (castle)'.

b_belz.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1030 when Yaroslav the Wise recaptured Belz from the Poles (also referenced retrospectively as part of the Cherven Cities region in 981).
b_belz.etymology_analysis: Derived from an Old Slavic root (*bъlzъ / *belzъ) denoting a damp, marshy lowland between the Solokiya and Richytsia rivers (with alternative hypotheses linking it to a personal name or Celtic/Gothic substrate).

b_liubachev.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written documents in 1214 (Spiš Treaty between Leszek I the White and Andrew II of Hungary) as Lubacew.
b_liubachev.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym formed from the Slavic personal name *Ljubacь / *Ljubach (from *ljubъ 'dear, beloved') with the possessive suffix -evъ (later Polonized to -ów).

b_cherven_VOL.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 981 AD, when Vladimir the Great marched against the Lyakhs and took Peremyshl, Cherven, and other towns.
b_cherven_VOL.etymology_analysis: Derived from Proto-Slavic *čьrvenъ ('red', from *čьrvь 'worm', referring to the Polish cochineal insect Porphyrophora polonica used for red dye), designating the principal fortified gord of the Cherven Cities.

b_volin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1018 AD as Velin' (Волынь/Велынь) during the campaign of Bolesław I the Brave and Sviatopolk against Yaroslav the Wise on the Bug River.

morphemes.translation: wet, moist, marshy (or tribal ethnonym Volhynians)

b_volin.etymology_analysis: Identified with the early medieval gord at Gródek nad Bugiem; derived either from the Slavic root *vel-/*vol- ('wet, marshy lowland') or the tribal name of the Volhynians (Velinjane).

b_kholm.first_mention_attestation: Founded and fortified in 1237 by Prince Daniel Romanovich of Galicia–Volhynia (with town rights noted in 1233–1237 in regional historiography).
b_kholm.etymology_analysis: Directly from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ ('hill'), referring to the prominent chalk hill (Góra Chełmska) on which Daniel of Galicia built the citadel.

b_suteysk.first_mention_attestation: Fortified gord established c. 1034–1039 by Yaroslav the Wise and first attested in the Primary Chronicle under 1097 AD.
b_suteysk.etymology_analysis: From Proto-Slavic *sъtěskъ ('narrow passage, defile', referring to the constriction of the Wieprz/Por valley near modern Sąsiadka) with the toponymic suffix -ьskъ.

b_peremyshl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 981 AD when Vladimir the Great captured Peremyshl and Cherven from the Lyakhs.
b_peremyshl.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the unattested early Slavic personal name *Peremyslъ ('forethought, provident one') + possessive suffix *-jь (yielding Peremyšl' / Przemyśl).

b_yaroslav_VOL.first_mention_attestation: First confirmed written mention in 1152 (traditionally founded in 1031 by Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise).
b_yaroslav_VOL.eponym_details: Named after Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise (Yaroslav Vladimirovich, r. 1019–1054), who according to tradition founded the stronghold in 1031.
b_yaroslav_VOL.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Christian/princely name Yaroslav (Old East Slavic Jaroslavъ) + possessive suffix *-jь, yielding Jarosławl' / Jarosław.

b_sanok.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1150 AD as a fortified Ruthenian stronghold on the San River.
b_sanok.etymology_analysis: Settlement name derived from the hydronym of the San River (with Slavic diminutive/relational suffix -okъ), denoting the town situated on the San.

b_lizhensk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1346 (and granted Magdeburg town rights in 1397 by King Władysław II Jagiełło).

morphemes.translation: settlement on a low-lying / resting place (or personal name)

b_lizhensk.etymology_analysis: Old Polish toponym (Leżajsk, East Slavic Lizhensk) formed with the suffix -sk from a root related to *ležati ('to lie, low-lying ground') or an unattested personal name.

b_halych.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned for the year 898 in the Hungarian chronicle Gesta Hungarorum (later attested in East Slavic chronicles in the 12th century, e.g., 1140).
b_halych.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived either from Slavic *galica ('jackdaw', reflected in the city's heraldry) or from an Indo-European/Greek root *hal- ('salt') referring to local salt springs, with the suffix -ičь.

b_sambir.first_mention_attestation: Original settlement (modern Staryi Sambir) attested by 1241 (destroyed during the Mongol invasion, after which survivors founded New Sambir; Staryi Sambir is also documented in 1378).
b_sambir.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Slavic *sąborъ / *samborъ (alternatively linked to a personal name Sambor or a wetland/willow/pine-forest term along the upper Dniester).

b_kolomyia.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1240 in the Galician–Volhynian Chronicle as a salt-trading town in Pokuttia.
b_kolomyia.etymology_analysis: Ukrainian etymological dictionaries derive Kolomyia from Proto-Slavic *kolo ('wheel') + *myti ('to wash'), referring to washing cart wheels or salt-carriages at the Prut River crossing (with alternative theories linking it to a personal name Kolomyi).

b_spas.first_mention_attestation: Attested since at least 1295 AD; Prince Leo I of Galicia died at the Spas residence/monastery complex in 1301.
b_spas.etymology_analysis: Named after the Church/Monastery of the Savior (Spas, Old East Slavic Spasъ 'Savior'), which served as a fortified Carpathian residence of Prince Leo I of Galicia.

b_lviv.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Galician–Volhynian Chronicle under 1256 AD, founded by King Daniel of Galicia.
b_lviv.eponym_details: Named after Leo I of Galicia (Lev Danylovych, c. 1228–1301), eldest son of King Daniel of Ruthenia.
b_lviv.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Old East Slavic Lьvъ ('Leo/Lev') + possessive suffix -ovъ, meaning 'city of Lev' (Lviv / Lwów / Lemberg).

b_zvenyhorod.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle (Laurentian text) under 1086 AD (1087 in the Hypatian Chronicle) in connection with the murder of Prince Yaropolk Iziaslavich.
b_zvenyhorod.etymology_analysis: Compound Slavic toponym from *zveněti ('to ring, resound'—referring to alarm bells or resounding fame) + *gorodъ ('fortified town').

b_busk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1097 AD as Buzhsk (Old East Slavic бужьсъкъ городъ).
b_busk.etymology_analysis: Settlement name derived from the Western Bug River (Old East Slavic Bugъ -> adjectival stem Buž-) + toponymic suffix -ьskъ, yielding Buzhsk and modern Busk.

b_buchach.first_mention_attestation: Earliest recorded mention dates to 1260 AD (cited by Bartosz Paprocki; later securely documented in 14th-century Polish charters).
b_buchach.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *bukъ ('beech tree', via *bučina 'beech grove') or *bučati ('to roar, rush', referring to the Strypa River) with the suffix -ačь.

b_moklekov.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle (Galician–Volhynian Chronicle) under 1211 AD (in the campaign of Leszek the White and Daniel Romanovich toward Halych).
b_moklekov.etymology_analysis: Possessive East Slavic oikonym formed from an unattested personal name *Moklekъ (related to *mokl- / *mokryj 'wet') with the possessive suffix -ovъ (-iv).

b_terebovl.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1097 AD as Terebovl' (seat of Prince Vasilko Rostislavich).
b_terebovl.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *terebiti ('to clear land, uproot trees') or a personal name *Terebovъ with the possessive suffix *-jь (yielding Terebovl').

b_horodok.first_mention_attestation: Horodok in Ternopil Oblast (at the confluence of the Seret and Dniester rivers) has its first written mention in 1418 AD.
b_horodok.etymology_analysis: East Slavic diminutive of *gorodъ ('fortified town'), meaning 'little town' or 'small fortress' (Ukrainian Horodok).

b_chortkiv.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written sources in 1427 (and granted Magdeburg town rights in 1522 by King Sigismund I the Old to Jerzy Czortkowski).
b_chortkiv.eponym_details: In 1522 King Sigismund I the Old granted ownership to Polish nobleman Jerzy Czortkowski and permitted him to name the town after himself (Czortków / Chortkiv).
b_chortkiv.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym officially named in 1522 after its proprietor Jerzy Czortkowski (Polish Czortków, Ukrainian Chortkiv).

b_zaslavl.first_mention_attestation: Zaslav (modern Iziaslav in Volhynia) was first mentioned in written records in 1390 AD (though archaeological remains date back to the 11th century).
b_zaslavl.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 Rurikid prince Iziaslav (shortened to Zaslav), founder of the Volhynian stronghold.
b_zaslavl.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old East Slavic princely name Izjaslavъ + *-jь, yielding Izjaslavl' and contracted Zaslavl' / Zaslav.

b_dubno.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary/Hypatian Chronicle under 1100 AD as Duben, in the possession of David Igorevich.
b_dubno.etymology_analysis: Derived from Proto-Slavic *dąbъ ('oak') + suffix -ьno/-no, denoting a settlement situated amid oak forests.

b_ostroh.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1100 AD as a Volhynian fortress.
b_ostroh.etymology_analysis: Directly from Old East Slavic ostrogъ (Proto-Slavic *ostrogъ 'wooden palisade, stockade fort', from *ostrъ 'sharp').

b_berestye.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 1019 AD (also cited as 1017 in some chronicle variants) as Berestye.
b_berestye.etymology_analysis: Collective toponym from Proto-Slavic *berstъ ('elm tree') or *beresta ('birch bark') + collective suffix -ьje, denoting a place rich in elms or birch.

b_bielsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Codex under 1253 AD as the gord of Bielsk.
b_bielsk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Proto-Slavic *bělъ ('white', likely via the Biała River or chalky/white terrain) + toponymic suffix -ьskъ.

b_kamyanyets.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Galician–Volhynian Chronicle under 1276 AD, when Prince Vladimir Vasilkovich ordered the architect Oleksa to build a stone keep here.
b_kamyanyets.etymology_analysis: Derived from East Slavic kamenь ('stone') + suffix -ecь, referring to the stony bank of the Lesnaya River and the famous stone tower built in 1276.

b_simiatychi.first_mention_attestation: History dates back to the mid-16th century; King Sigismund II Augustus granted Siemiatycze its town charter in 1542 AD.
b_simiatychi.etymology_analysis: Patronymic plural toponym derived from the Slavic personal name *Semjata (*Siemięta) + -iči (-ycze), meaning 'settlement of Semjata's kin/people'.

b_dorohychyn.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Rus' chronicles in 1061 AD (and prominently in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1142 AD as a frontier gord).
b_dorohychyn.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from a Slavic personal name *Dorogičь / *Drogicz + -inъ (alternatively linked to *doroga 'road/trade route' along the Bug River).

b_kobryn.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1287 AD in the testament of Prince Vladimir Vasilkovich of Volhynia.
b_kobryn.etymology_analysis: Derived either from a Slavic personal name *Kobrъ + possessive suffix -inъ, or from *kъ obr- ('to the Obry/Avars') reflecting early medieval ethnic memory.

b_blotkowo.first_mention_attestation: Village of Błotków (Błotkowo, later the site of Terespol) first attested in 1512 AD.
b_blotkowo.etymology_analysis: Topographic-derived settlement name from Polish błoto ('mud, marsh') + toponymic suffix -kowo/-ków, reflecting the marshy floodplain of the Bug River opposite Brest.

b_peresopnytsia.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1147 AD (seat of Prince Viacheslav I of Kiev in 1147–1149).
b_peresopnytsia.etymology_analysis: Derived from East Slavic *pere-sъp- ('crossed embankment / earthen rampart') + suffix -nica, referring to the fortified earthen earthworks on the Stubla River.

b_rivne.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1283 AD (in the Rocznik kapituły krakowskiej regarding a battle between Leszek II the Black and Lithuanian forces).
b_rivne.etymology_analysis: Substantivized neuter adjective from Proto-Slavic *rovьnъ ('flat, level'), describing a settlement situated on a flat, level plain (Ukrainian Rivne, Polish Równe).

b_klevan.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of the name Klevan appeared in 1458 AD as a possession of the Czartoryski family (an earlier 12th-century settlement on the site was known as Kolyvan).
b_klevan.etymology_analysis: Evolved from the 12th-century settlement name Kolyvan (Kolivan) to Klevan by 1458; variously linked to Slavic *klevъ ('enclosure, cattle shed') or an unattested personal name.

b_volodymyr.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 988 AD, when Grand Prince Vladimir the Great founded/named the city and gave it to his son Vsevolod.
b_volodymyr.eponym_details: Named after Grand Prince Vladimir the Great (Volodymyr Sviatoslavych, c. 958–1015).
b_volodymyr.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old East Slavic princely name Volodimerъ ('Vladimir/Volodymyr') + possessive suffix *-jь, yielding Volodimer' (Latinized Lodomeria).

b_lutsk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle under 1085 AD as Luchesk (Луческ).

morphemes.translation: river bend, meadow (or tribal name Luchane)

b_lutsk.etymology_analysis: From Old East Slavic Lučeskъ, derived either from *luka ('bend in a river', referring to the Styr River) or the Slavic tribal branch Luchane + toponymic suffix -ьskъ.

b_luboml.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Hypatian Chronicle in 1287 AD as a favourite residence of Prince Vladimir Vasilkovich of Volhynia.
b_luboml.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from an unattested Slavic personal name *Ljubomyslъ (or *Ljubomilъ) + possessive suffix *-jь, contracted to Ljuboml' / Liuboml.

b_kovel.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1310 AD (received Magdeburg town charter in 1518 from King Sigismund I the Old).
b_kovel.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavic occupational noun *kovalь / *kovelь ('blacksmith'), reflected in the horseshoe on Kovel's municipal coat of arms.

b_rozhyshche.first_mention_attestation: First written mention dates to 1322 AD, when Prince Liubart Gediminovich of Lutsk donated it to the cathedral church of St. John the Theologian.
b_rozhyshche.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *rogъ ('horn, corner, promontory/bend of the Styr River') with the locative suffix -išče.

b_brno.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Cosmas' Chronica Boemorum under 1091, when King Vratislaus II besieged his brother Conrad at Brno Castle.
b_brno.etymology_analysis: Disputed origin: either from Old Czech brnie ('muddy, swampy'), from the Slavic verb brniti ('to armour, fortify'), or a Celtic cognate of *briga / bryn ('hill'). Precursor Great Moravian hillfort Staré Zámky existed nearby, but no pre-867 written name is attested.

older_name_by_867.notes: Great Moravian hillfort Staré Zámky at Brno-Líšeň existed in the 9th century, but no contemporary written name <= 867 AD is attested.

b_ivancice.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Ivančice dates to 1212; became a royal town under King Wenceslaus II in 1288.
b_ivancice.etymology_analysis: Derived from the personal name Ivanek (a diminutive of Ivan) with the Slavic patronymic suffix -ice, meaning 'the village of Ivanek's people'.

b_zdar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1253 following the founding of the Cistercian monastery (1252) on the Sázava River.
b_zdar.etymology_analysis: From Old Czech žďár ('burned clearing'), referring to slash-and-burn land clearance during 13th-century colonization. The Sázava River itself is first attested in 1045.

older_name_by_867.notes: The Sázava River is first attested in 1045, also post-867.

b_jihlava.first_mention_attestation: Town first mentioned in writing in 1233 (the Jihlava river as Giglaue in 1226).
b_jihlava.etymology_analysis: Named after the Jihlava River (first attested 1226 as Giglaue), whose name is derived either from Slavic jehla ('needle', referring to sharp stones in the riverbed) or German Igel ('hedgehog').

b_telcz.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in 1335 (local legend claims 1099 foundation).
b_telcz.etymology_analysis: Originally Teleč, formed by adding the Slavic possessive suffix to the personal name Telec ('young calf').

b_olomouc.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1017 (Thietmar of Merseburg; later in Cosmas under 1055).
b_olomouc.etymology_analysis: Origin uncertain; most commonly derived from a Slavic personal name Olmút ('Olmút's castle/court'), or alternatively from Proto-Slavic *ol ('beer') and *mútit ('to stir/make noise').

older_name_by_867.notes: Renaissance legend of Roman 'Iuliomontium' is unconfirmed; Roman marching camps existed nearby without a confirmed ancient settlement name.

b_unicov.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a royal town around 1213 on the site of an earlier village.
b_unicov.etymology_analysis: Derived from the personal name Unič with the possessive suffix -ov. Also known in Latin as Nova civitas and German as Mährisch Neustadt ('Moravian New Town').

b_kromeriz.first_mention_attestation: First written mention as Cromezir in a deed dated between 1107 and 1125 when bought by Bishop John II of Olomouc.
b_kromeriz.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the Old Slavic personal name Kroměžir.

b_prerov.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in 1141 in a charter of Bishop Jindřich Zdík of Olomouc.
b_prerov.etymology_analysis: From Proto-Slavic / Old Czech přerov meaning 'ditch', 'pool', or 'swamp', referring to a moated or marshy site.

b_spytihnev.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of the settlement/castle in 1131 (and 1141) in Bishop Jindřich Zdík's charter.
b_spytihnev.eponym_details: Named after Duke Spytihněv II of Bohemia (r. 1055–1061), who established or fortified the border castle.
b_spytihnev.etymology_analysis: Named after Duke Spytihněv II of Bohemia (11th century); the Slavic personal name Spytihněv combines spyti- and hněv ('wrath').

b_hodonin.first_mention_attestation: First credible written mention of Hodonín dates to 1169; elevated to a town in 1228.
b_hodonin.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Czech personal name Hodona with the possessive suffix -ín ('Hodona's property/settlement').

b_veseli.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Veselí (nad Moravou) dates to 1261, when a water castle and settlement existed there.
b_veseli.etymology_analysis: From Czech veselý / veselí ('cheerful, merry'), a common Slavic settlement name denoting a pleasant or lively location.

b_znojmo.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of the royal town of Znojmo is from 1226 (though Znojmo Castle was founded by Přemyslid dukes in the 11th century).

morphemes.translation: heat ('exposed to heat') OR personal name Znojem/Znojim

b_znojmo.etymology_analysis: Uncertain origin: either from Old Czech znoj ('heat', i.e., a sun-exposed site) or possessive from the personal name Znojem/Znojim.

older_name_by_867.notes: Archaeological Great Moravian hillfort existed at Hradiště sv. Hypolita, but no pre-867 written name is attested.

b_bitov.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Bítov is in the foundation deed of the Stará Boleslav Chapter from 1046 (castle mentioned in the 1060s).
b_bitov.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the Old Slavic personal name Bít (Germanized as Vöttau).

b_breclav.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1056; named after its founder, Duke Bretislav I of Bohemia (r. 1034–1055).
b_breclav.eponym_details: Named after Duke Bretislav I of Bohemia (r. 1034–1055), who founded Břeclav Castle.
b_breclav.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Czech name of Duke Bretislav I (Břetislav), founder of the local border castle in the 11th century.

older_name_by_867.notes: Nearby Great Moravian center Pohansko flourished in the 9th century, but its contemporary name <= 867 AD is not attested.

b_mikulov.first_mention_attestation: First trustworthy written mention in 1249 in a deed by Margrave Ottokar II granting the castle to Henry I of Liechtenstein (a 1173 deed is a 14th-century hoax).
b_mikulov.etymology_analysis: Derived from the personal name Mikul (short for Mikuláš/Nicholas); historically known in German as Nikolsburg, with Czech Mikulov becoming standard in the 19th century.

b_bars.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1075 (Starý Tekov / Tekov Castle) in the founding charter of Hronský Beňadik Abbey.

morphemes.translation: personal name / noble clan name (Slovak: Tekov)

b_bars.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Bars (from Old Hungarian personal/clan name Bors/Bars); Slovak Tekov is attested alongside it for the castle and region at Starý Tekov.

older_name_by_867.notes: The nearby Hron River was attested in 170 AD as Granus by Marcus Aurelius, but Tekov/Bars itself is first attested in 1075.

b_komorcbanya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1328 when King Charles Robert of Hungary granted Kremnica free royal town privileges and established its mint.
b_komorcbanya.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Körmöcbánya combines Körmöc (adapted from Slavic Kremnica, from *kremen 'flint/quartz') with bánya ('mine'), reflecting its medieval gold mining.

b_gemer.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical records in 1198 as Gomur (1216 Gumur, 1289 Gemer) in the Gesta Hungarorum.
b_gemer.etymology_analysis: Associated by János Melich and Lajos Kiss with Old Turkic kömür ('coal') or the Turkic personal name Kemirbaj; a Slavic fortified settlement preceded the medieval castle.

b_murany.first_mention_attestation: Village first mentioned in 1321 as a settlement beneath Muráň Castle (castle built in the 13th century).
b_murany.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic múr ('wall'), referring either to the steep rocky cliff wall of the Cigánka massif or the stone fortress built atop it in the 13th century.

b_rimaszombat.first_mention_attestation: First written record in 1268 as Rymoa Zumbota, belonging to the Archbishopric of Kalocsa.
b_rimaszombat.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Rimava River (Hungarian Rima) and szombat ('Saturday', from Slavic sobota), referring to the town's weekly Saturday market.

b_hont.first_mention_attestation: Settlement and castle founded at the turn of the 10th and 11th centuries by Hunt (fl. 997); Hont Castle is attested in 12th-century charters such as 1135.
b_hont.eponym_details: Named after Hunt (Cuntio), a Swabian/German knight who settled in Hungary at the turn of the 10th–11th centuries and sheltered Stephen I in 997.
b_hont.etymology_analysis: Named after Hunt (Old German 'captain'), who built the earthwork fortress on the Ipeľ peninsula around 1000 AD, giving his name to Hont County and the village.

b_nograd.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1108 (and 1138 as civitas Naugrad).
b_nograd.etymology_analysis: Hungarian adaptation of Slavic Novgrad / Novigrad ('New Castle'), corresponding to Slovak Novohrad.

morphemes.translation: name of one of the seven Magyar tribes

b_balassagyarmat.etymology_analysis: Named after the conquering Hungarian Gyarmat tribe, with the prefix Balassa- added later from the Balassa noble family.

b_koporna.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1135 in the founding charter of Bzovík Monastery (Korpona / Krupina).

morphemes.translation: solid, strong / small fortress, or coarse/rocky

b_koporna.etymology_analysis: Korpona (modern Slovak Krupina; misspelled Koporna in repo) derives from Proto-Slavic *krǫpъ ('solid, strong' or 'coarse/rocky'), either referring to a small fortified settlement or the rocky riverbed of the Krupinica.

b_losonc.first_mention_attestation: First indirect mention in 1128 (when Lambert built a chapel to the Virgin Mary); first direct mention of the settlement in 1247 as Luchunch.

morphemes.translation: meadowy place (from lúka 'meadow') or personal name Lučan

b_losonc.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Losonc (Slovak Lučenec) is a Slavic-derived toponym, commonly linked to lúka ('meadow') or a personal name Lučan.

b_selmecbanya.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1156 as terra banensium ('land of miners').
b_selmecbanya.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Selmecbánya combines Selmec (adapted from Slavic Štiavnica, 'acidic spring') with bánya ('mine'), reflecting its medieval silver mining.

b_liptoujvar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1341, named after the nearby Liptovský Hrádok castle.

morphemes.translation: Liptov region (from Slavic personal name Ľubota)

b_liptoujvar.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Liptóújvár means 'New Castle of Liptov' (corresponding to Slovak Liptovský Hrádok, 'Little Castle of Liptov'). Liptov itself is first attested in 1231.

b_nemetlipsce.first_mention_attestation: Poprad (the input modern_name) is first mentioned in 1250; note that the barony key b_nemetlipsce corresponds to Partizánska Ľupča (Németlipcse), first mentioned in 1252.
b_nemetlipsce.etymology_analysis: Poprad is named after the Poprad River, derived from the Proto-Slavic verb *pręd- ('to flow swiftly'). (The key b_nemetlipsce originally referred to Németlipcse / Partizánska Ľupča, attested 1252, from Slavic personal name Ľub-).

b_nyitra.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum (recording the c. 828 consecration of a church in Nitrava by Archbishop Adalram of Salzburg for Prince Pribina).
b_nyitra.etymology_analysis: Derived directly from the Nitra River, an Indo-European/pre-Slavic hydronym adapted into Slavic as Nitrava / Nitra (Hungarian: Nyitra).

older_name_by_867.notes: Already attested as Nitrava in c. 828 AD.

b_pecsen.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Pečeňady dates to 1208 as villa Bissenorum ('village of the Pechenegs').
b_pecsen.etymology_analysis: Named after the Pechenegs (Latin Bisseni, Slovak Pečenehovia), who were settled in the Kingdom of Hungary as border guards in the 11th–12th centuries.

b_bajmoc.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1113 in the Zobor Abbey charter.
b_bajmoc.etymology_analysis: Bojnice (Hungarian Bajmóc) derives either from Slavic boj ('battle/battleground') or from a Slavic personal name such as Bojan/Bojma.

b_sasvar.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Šaštín (Sasvár) dates to 1218.
b_sasvar.etymology_analysis: Slovak Šaštín combines šáš ('sedge') and týn ('fence, small fort'); Hungarian Sasvár ('sedge-castle' or folk-etymologized 'eagle-castle') translates/adapts the same elements.

b_arva.first_mention_attestation: First written record of Orava Castle dates to 1267 (the Orava River is first recorded in 1287 as fl. Arua).
b_arva.etymology_analysis: Named after the Orava River (Hungarian Árva), from Pre-Slavic *er-/*or- ('swift') or Proto-Slavic *orati ('to roar') with the hydronymic suffix -ava.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Púchov culture hillforts existed in the Orava valley, but no written name <= 867 AD is attested.

b_twardosczino.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Tvrdošín dates to 1265.
b_twardosczino.etymology_analysis: Possessive formation from the Slavic personal name Tvrdoš (derived from tvrdý 'hard, firm').

b_poszony.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 907 AD in the Annales Iuvavenses as Brezalauspurc (Battle of Pressburg); Pozsony is first attested in 1002.
b_poszony.eponym_details: Brezalauspurc ('Braslav's castle') is named after Braslav, Duke of Lower Pannonia (fl. 884–896); Pozsony is attributed to a 10th-century prince/noble Božan (before 950).
b_poszony.etymology_analysis: Attested as Brezalauspurc in 907 (named after Duke Braslav) and Poson/Pozsony in 1002 (from Slavic personal name Božan); modern Bratislava was coined in the 19th century.

older_name_by_867.notes: Great Moravian hillfort existed on Bratislava Castle hill in the 9th century, but its first written attestation is 907 AD.

b_smozolany.first_mention_attestation: First documented in 1256 as villa Solmus.
b_smozolany.etymology_analysis: Smolenice (Hungarian Szomolány; Smozolany in repo) is derived from smoliari ('makers/collectors of pitch/tar').

older_name_by_867.notes: Hallstatt hillfort Molpír stood nearby in the 1st millennium BCE, but no written name <= 867 AD is attested.

b_somorja.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1238 as ecclesia Sancte Mariae (and 1285 as villa Sancti Marie).

morphemes.translation: Saint Mary (patron saint of the local church)

b_somorja.etymology_analysis: Derived from the patron saint of the local church, Sancta Maria (Hungarian Zent Maria > Samaria > Somorja, Slovakized as Šamorín).

b_trenscen.first_mention_attestation: The medieval name Trenčín (Trencinium) is first attested in the Zobor Charter of 1111, though the same site is attested in Antiquity as Leukaristos (c. 150 AD) and Laugaricio (179 AD).
b_trenscen.etymology_analysis: Medieval/modern Trenčín (Hungarian Trencsén) is likely a possessive form from a Slavic personal name; the castle rock bears a 179 AD Roman inscription naming the settlement Laugaricio (Ptolemy's Leukaristos, c. 150 AD).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 AD, as Leukaristos) and the 179 AD Roman inscription at Trenčín Castle rock (Laugaricio)
older_name_by_867.notes: Laugaricio is explicitly inscribed on the rock below Trenčín Castle (179 AD) and identified with Ptolemy's Leukaristos (c. 150 AD).

b_puho.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Púchov dates to 1243.

morphemes.translation: personal name Púch OR burial place

b_puho.etymology_analysis: Derived either from a Slavic personal name Púch with possessive suffix -ov, or from pochov ('burial place', referencing ancient graves excavated at Púchovská skala).

older_name_by_867.notes: Prehistoric/Iron Age Púchov culture site, but no written name <= 867 AD is attested.

b_zsolna.first_mention_attestation: First written reference to Žilina (Zsolna) dates to 1208 as terra de Selinan.
b_zsolna.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic žila ('river vein, watercourse'), meaning 'a place with many watercourses' (at the confluence of the Váh, Kysuca, and Rajčanka), or from the Žilinka stream.

b_turoc.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1113 as Turc in the Zobor Charter (referring to the Turiec River and region).

morphemes.translation: diminutive/derivative of tur ('aurochs') or pre-Slavic hydronym

b_turoc.etymology_analysis: Hungarian Turóc derives from Old Slavic *Turъcь (1113 Turc), the name of the Turiec River (linked by some to Slavic tur 'aurochs', or anciently compared to Pliny's Durius).

b_zolyom.first_mention_attestation: Earliest written mention of Zvolen (Zólyom) dates to 1135.
b_zolyom.etymology_analysis: Of Slavic origin, meaning 'the chosen [place]' (Latinized as Zolium, Hungarian Zólyom).

b_breznobanya.first_mention_attestation: First written evidence dates to 1265 in a charter of King Béla IV of Hungary mentioning the settlement Berezuno.
b_breznobanya.etymology_analysis: Slovak Brezno derives from breza ('birch'); the Hungarian name Breznóbánya appends bánya ('mine').

b_opava.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of the town of Opava dates to 1195; received town rights in 1224.
b_opava.etymology_analysis: Named after the Opava River, whose name derives from an ancient Indo-European/Celtic root *apa / *opa ('water') with the hydronymic suffix -ava.

b_hradec-nad-moravici.first_mention_attestation: First written mention of Hradec and its fortress dates to 1060, when Bolesław II the Generous's army was defeated there (gord built in the 8th century).
b_hradec-nad-moravici.etymology_analysis: Hradec is a diminutive of Czech hrad ('castle'); the river locator nad Moravicí ('upon the Moravice') was added in 1972.

older_name_by_867.notes: A Slavic gord existed in the 8th century, but no written name <= 867 AD is attested.

b_dobrzyn.first_mention_attestation: 1065 AD (as 'Dobrin' in the Mogilno Falsification, Falsyfikat mogileński)
b_dobrzyn.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Dobr (or Dobry) or the adjective dobry ('good') with the possessive/toponymic suffix -yń, denoting a settlement associated with Dobr.

b_michalowo.first_mention_attestation: 1240 AD (attested as the seat of a castellany in Kuyavian-Masovian charters; archaeological settlement from 12th century)
b_michalowo.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym formed from the Polish personal name Michał (Michael) and the suffix -owo, denoting a settlement belonging to Michał.

b_kruszwica.first_mention_attestation: 1093 AD (recorded as 'Crusvicz' in Gallus Anonymus's Cronica Polonorum describing the 1093–1096 conflict)
b_kruszwica.etymology_analysis: Slavic toponym derived either from Proto-Slavic *gruša ('pear tree') or *krušiti / kruszyć ('to break/salt lump', referencing local salt springs), with the suffix -wica.

b_wloclawek.first_mention_attestation: 1112–1116 AD (recorded as 'Wladislau castro' in Gallus Anonymus's Cronica Polonorum)
b_wloclawek.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Polish male personal name Włodzisław / Władysław (originally Władysławia, 'Władysław's stronghold'), later altered with the diminutive suffix -ek to Włocławek.

b_inowroclaw.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as Novo Wladislaw (1185) and Juveni Wladislawia (1236, 'Young/New Władysław'), likely named after settlers from Włocławek or in honor of Duke Władysław I Herman; later Polonized to Inowrocław.

b_bydgoszcz.first_mention_attestation: 1238 AD (first mentioned as a castellany; 1239 'Bidgosciam', 1242 'castrum quod Budegosta vulgariter nuncupatur')
b_bydgoszcz.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Old Polish personal name Bydgost (composed of *bъd- 'to wake/watch' and *gostь 'guest/host') with the possessive suffix -ja, yielding Bydgoszcza, later Bydgoszcz.

b_leczyca.first_mention_attestation: 1112–1116 AD (recorded as 'Lucic' in Gallus Anonymus's Cronica Polonorum; 1136 'Lancicia' in the Bull of Gniezno)
b_leczyca.etymology_analysis: Derived either from the West Slavic tribe of the Łęczanie or from Old Polish łęg ('swampy plain, marshy meadow') with the suffix -ica, reflecting the wetland terrain along the Bzura River.

morphemes.translation: boat (or related to łoza 'willow' / river Łódka)

b_lodz.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1332 as Lodza/Lodzia; linguists link the name either to Old Polish łodzia/łódź ('boat'), łoza ('willow tree'), the River Łódka, or a shortened form of the personal name Włodzisław.

b_klodawa.first_mention_attestation: 1430 AD (town charter; 11th-century church foundation attributed to Władysław I Herman without contemporary 11th-c. charter)
b_klodawa.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish kłoda ('log, fallen tree' or timbered forest lair) with the suffix -awa, also associated with the local stream (Kłodawica / Rgilewka).

b_sieradz.first_mention_attestation: 1136 AD (recorded as 'Ziraz' in the Bull of Gniezno)

morphemes.translation: Slavic personal name (from Wszerad or Sirorad)

b_sieradz.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym formed from the Old Polish personal name Sirad/Sierad (shortened from Wszerad or Sirorad) with the palatalizing possessive suffix *-jь, yielding Sieradz.

b_piotrkow.first_mention_attestation: 13th century (1217 AD earliest ducal document mention as 'Piotrków' / 'Pietrków')
b_piotrkow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Piotrek (diminutive of Piotr, 'Peter') + -ów. Local tradition attributes its founding to 12th-century magnate Piotr Włostowic, though this is unconfirmed in contemporary sources.

b_przedborz.first_mention_attestation: 1136 AD (recorded as 'Predbor' / 'Przedbórz' in 12th-century records; town charter before 1370)
b_przedborz.etymology_analysis: Either a topographic name from przed borem ('in front of the wilderness/forest', referring to the Pilica and Świętokrzyska forests) or a possessive name from the Old Polish personal name Przedbor.

b_radomsko.first_mention_attestation: 1243 AD (oldest known mention in a document of Duke Konrad I of Masovia)
b_radomsko.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Radom (or Radomir) with the toponymic suffix -sko (attested in medieval forms as Radomokye, Radomsk, Radomskie).

b_uniejow.first_mention_attestation: 1136 AD (recorded as 'Uneievo' / 'Unieievo' in the Bull of Gniezno of Pope Innocent II)
b_uniejow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Old Polish personal name Uniej (meaning 'better' or 'younger') with the suffix -ów.

b_wielun.first_mention_attestation: 1282 AD (first mentioned as 'Velun'; preceded as regional seat by Ruda, attested 1136 AD)
b_wielun.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1282 as Velun; either derived from a Slavic root *vel- denoting wetness/wetland (as noted by Jan Długosz) or from the Old Polish personal name Wielisław.

b_grabow.first_mention_attestation: 1264 AD (first mentioned in historical records as 'Grabów')
b_grabow.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Polish tree name grab ('hornbeam') with the toponymic suffix -ów, indicating a settlement near hornbeam woods.

b_krakow.first_mention_attestation: 966 AD (first written mention by Ibrahim ibn Yaqub as 'Karākū' / Kraków; 973 AD 'Cracoua' in Latin documents)
b_krakow.etymology_analysis: Archaic Polish possessive form of the personal name Krak (traditionally the legendary founder Krakus of the Vistulans) with -ów, though linguists also debate pre-Slavic or topographic roots.

b_olsztyn.first_mention_attestation: Early 14th century (c. 1306 AD; castle and settlement attested as 'Holsztyn' / 'Hohlstein')
b_olsztyn.etymology_analysis: Polonized from earlier Holsztyn, from German Hohlstein ('hollow stone/rock with a cave', referring to the limestone cave beneath the castle) or Holstein (origin of German settlers).

b_czestochowa.first_mention_attestation: 1220 AD (recorded as 'Czanstochowa' in a document of Bishop Iwo Odrowąż of Kraków)
b_czestochowa.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Old Polish personal name Częstoch (a hypocoristic of Częstobor or Częstomir) with the feminine possessive suffix -owa, meaning 'Częstoch's place'.

b_dabrowa_gorn.first_mention_attestation: 1652–1655 AD (village founded c. 1652 as 'Koniecpolska Wola'; name 'Dąbrowa' first attested in 1655 parish records in Będzin)
b_dabrowa_gorn.etymology_analysis: Named after Polish dąbrowa ('oak grove', from dąb 'oak'), reflecting the original forested terrain; the adjective Górnicza ('mining') was added in the 19th century due to coal mining.

b_wislica.first_mention_attestation: 1166 AD (capital of the Duchy of Wiślica 1166–1173; earlier 9th-c. Vita Methodii mentions the Vistulan prince without naming Wiślica)
b_wislica.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavic root *visl- (water/spring/wetland, related to Wisła/Vistula and medieval wiślica 'spring or spring-flooded area') with the suffix -ica; legend links it to prince Wiślimir.

b_jedrzejow.first_mention_attestation: 1153 AD (settlement of Brzeznica/Jędrzejów mentioned in the 1153 foundation charter of the Cistercian abbey by Archbishop Janik of Gniezno)
b_jedrzejow.etymology_analysis: Earlier attested as Brzeznica (1153); later renamed Andrzejów / Jędrzejów after a member of the local Lis noble family named Andrzej (Jędrzej).

b_lublin.first_mention_attestation: 1228 AD (name 'Lublin' first appears in written sources in 1228; castellany from 12th century)
b_lublin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Old Polish personal name Lubla (hypocoristic of Lubomir) with the possessive suffix -in.

b_parczew.first_mention_attestation: 1235 AD (attested by Jan Długosz as existing in 1235; town charter in 1401)
b_parczew.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym formed from the Old Polish male personal name Parcz with the suffix -ew (also recorded as Parczów).

b_goraj.first_mention_attestation: 1373 AD (person 'Demetrio de Goray' mentioned; 1377 'castrum nostrum Goray alio Lada')
b_goraj.etymology_analysis: Topographic name meaning 'mountainous or hilly place', derived from Polish góra ('mountain, hill') reflecting its location among the Roztocze hills.

b_urzedow.first_mention_attestation: 1405 AD (first historical mention when King Władysław II Jagiełło granted Magdeburg rights, replacing villages Zaborzyce and Skorczyce)
b_urzedow.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish urząd ('office/official seat') with -ów, reflecting its foundation as a royal administrative and market center.

b_radom.first_mention_attestation: 1155 AD (first written mention in the bull of Pope Adrian IV)
b_radom.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Radom (shortened from Radomir) with the possessive suffix *-jь; folk etymology connects it to 'rad dom' ('gladly a home').

b_opoczno.first_mention_attestation: 1191 AD (mention of wooden Church of St. Mary Magdalene; 1284 AD explicit mention of 'Opoczno')
b_opoczno.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish opoka ('limestone, rocky outcrop') with the suffix -no, referring to the local stone terrain.

b_ilza.first_mention_attestation: 12th century (attested as property of the Bishops of Kraków from the 12th century; town charter c. 1294)
b_ilza.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Slavic root *il- / Polish ił ('clay, loam'), related to the Iłżanka River and local clay deposits.

b_szydlowiec.first_mention_attestation: 1401 AD (earliest documented mention of the name Szydłowiec)

morphemes.translation: place name (from szydło 'awl' or personal name)

b_szydlowiec.etymology_analysis: Diminutive toponym derived from Szydłów with the suffix -ec (the Odrowąż owners later took the surname Szydłowiecki from the town, not vice versa).

b_sacz.first_mention_attestation: 1257 AD (first mention of Sącz when Duke Bolesław V the Chaste granted the Sącz land to Duchess Kinga)
b_sacz.etymology_analysis: Historically Sądecz (later Sącz), derived from an Old Polish personal name Sędek/Sądek with the possessive suffix *-jь; Stary Sącz ('Old Sącz') was distinguished after Nowy Sącz was founded in 1292.

b_pilzno.first_mention_attestation: 1123–1125 AD (first mentioned in the document of Papal Legate Giles confirming possessions of Tyniec Abbey)
b_pilzno.etymology_analysis: According to Kazimierz Rymut, derived from the Slavic root *płz-/*pьlz- denoting slippery, wet ground (cognate with Czech Plzeň/Pilsen).

b_nowytarg.first_mention_attestation: 1233 AD (predecessor settlement 'Stare Cło' / Antiquum Theoloneum mentioned; Nowy Targ / Novum Forum chartered 1346)
b_nowytarg.etymology_analysis: Literally 'New Market' (Latin Novum Forum, Neoforum), founded in 1346 by Casimir III the Great beside the older customs settlement of Stare Cło (1233).

b_bochnia.first_mention_attestation: 1198 AD (first mentioned as 'Sal de Bochegna' in a letter of Patriarch Aymar confirming a donation by Mikora Gryfit)
b_bochnia.etymology_analysis: Contracted from older Bochynia (attested 1198 as Bochegna), derived from the Proto-Slavic root *boch- (common in hydronyms) with the suffix -ynia.

b_wieliczka.first_mention_attestation: 1123–1125 AD (first mentioned as 'Magnum Sal' ['Great Salt'] in the document of Papal Legate Giles)
b_wieliczka.etymology_analysis: Evolved from the medieval name Magnum Sal ('Great Salt', Polish Wielka Sól, attested 1123–1125), later shortened and suffixed to Wieliczka.

b_sandomierz.first_mention_attestation: 1112–1116 AD (recorded as 'Sandomir' in Gallus Anonymus's Cronica Polonorum as one of the sedes regni principales)
b_sandomierz.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym derived from the Old Polish personal name Sędomir (composed of sęd- 'judge' and mir 'peace') with the possessive suffix *-jь.

b_opatow.first_mention_attestation: 1189 AD (first mentioned in historical documents as a castellan seat)
b_opatow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym meaning 'Abbot's [town/estate]', from Polish opat ('abbot') + -ów, reflecting ecclesiastical/monastic ownership.

b_kielce.first_mention_attestation: 1171 AD (earliest extant document confirming the settlement and foundation of the collegiate church by Bishop Gedko of Kraków)
b_kielce.etymology_analysis: Most likely derived from Old Polish kielce (plural of kielec 'sprout'), referring to plants sprouting in the wetland terrain; legend links it to boar tusks (kły) found by Mieszko II.

b_olesnica_MPL.first_mention_attestation: 14th century (c. 1330–1358 AD; attested as seat of Zbigniew of Oleśnica; chartered 1470)
b_olesnica_MPL.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish olsza ('alder tree') with the suffix -nica, denoting an alder-grown place or stream.

b_checiny.first_mention_attestation: 1275 AD (first mentioned as a village/castle 'Chęcin' in historical documents)
b_checiny.etymology_analysis: Originally singular Chęcin (1275), likely a possessive name from an unattested Old Polish personal name *Chęta, pluralized to Chęciny in the 14th century to encompass the castle, village, and town.

b_stezyca.first_mention_attestation: 1325–1327 AD (first recorded as 'Stanzitia'; chartered 1330 by Casimir III the Great)
b_stezyca.etymology_analysis: Toponymic name associated with water/lakes/rivers (guarding a Vistula crossing), recorded in 1325–1327 as Stanzitia.

b_lukow.first_mention_attestation: 1233 AD (first mentioned as 'Castelani nostri de Lucow' in a document of Bolesław V the Chaste)
b_lukow.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Slavic łuk ('place located in a wetland / river bend') with the suffix -ów.

b_tarnow.etymology_analysis: Derived from Proto-Slavic *tъrnъ ('thorn, blackthorn') with the suffix -ów, denoting a thorny/scrubland settlement (cognate with Trnovo/Tarnau).

b_mielec.first_mention_attestation: 1229 AD (first mentioned in a bull of Pope Gregory IX)
b_mielec.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish miel ('shallow, shoal' in the Wisłoka river) or a related Slavic root with the suffix -ec.

b_baranow.first_mention_attestation: 1135 AD (first mentioned as a settlement/gord near a Vistula ford)
b_baranow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the personal name/nickname Baran ('ram') or from sheep husbandry (barany) with the suffix -ów; Sandomierski was added to distinguish it from other Baranóws.

b_breslau.first_mention_attestation: 1000 AD (recorded as 'Wrotizla' / 'Wortizlava' in Thietmar's Chronicle for the year 1000)
b_breslau.etymology_analysis: German Breslau adapts Polish Wrocław (earlier Wrocisław, attested 1000 AD in Thietmar as Wrotizla/Wortizlava), a possessive toponym from the personal name Wrocisław (traditionally linked to Vratislav I of Bohemia, though debated).

b_bardo.first_mention_attestation: 1096 AD (recorded as 'Brido' in Cosmas of Prague's Chronica Boemorum)
b_bardo.etymology_analysis: Topographic name directly from Proto-Slavic *bŕ̥do ('hill, ridge'), reflected in the 1096 attestation Brido and later Bardo (German Wartha, 'watchtower/guard post').

b_grunberg.first_mention_attestation: 1222 AD (traditional foundation date under Duke Henry I the Bearded; earliest town/church records 1294–1302; chartered 1323)
b_grunberg.etymology_analysis: German topographic/oronymic name Grünberg ('Green Mountain'), translated into Polish as Zielona Góra.

b_gubin.first_mention_attestation: 1211 AD (first mentioned in a document of Duke Henry I the Bearded)

morphemes.translation: bend, fold, or personal name Guba

b_gubin.etymology_analysis: Originally a Lower Sorbian/Slavic toponym Gubin (later Germanized as Guben), derived from a personal name Guba or Slavic *gub- ('bend/curve' of the Lusatian Neisse) with -in.

b_crossen.first_mention_attestation: 1005 AD (first mentioned as 'Crosno' in Thietmar's Chronicle during Bolesław I Chrobry's campaign)
b_crossen.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1005 as Crosno (Germanized as Crossen); derived from Polish krosno (though modern linguists reject Heinrich Adamy's 'weavers' town' gloss in favor of a topographic/structural meaning).

b_legnica.first_mention_attestation: 1004 AD (first referenced in chronicles dating from 1004 AD)
b_legnica.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish łęg ('wetland/floodplain meadow') or *leg- ('resting place') with -nica; Germanized as Liegnitz.

b_glogow.first_mention_attestation: 1010 AD (first mentioned in Thietmar's Chronicle as 'Glogua' / 'urbs Glogus')
b_glogow.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish głóg (glogh, 'hawthorn / thorny bush') with the suffix -ów, referring to hawthorn-covered terrain; Germanized as Glogau.

b_sadowel.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish sąd ('court, place of judgment', glossed by Heinrich Adamy as Gerichtsort), later Germanized as Sandelswalde.

b_miliez.first_mention_attestation: 1136 AD (recorded as 'Miliche' in the Bull of Gniezno of Pope Innocent II)
b_miliez.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Milik (from miły 'pleasant, friendly') with the suffix *-jь, meaning 'Milik's stronghold'; Germanized as Militsch.

b_olesnica.first_mention_attestation: 1189 AD (first mentioned as 'Olsznica' / trading settlement and abbey; 1214 'Oleznic')
b_olesnica.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish olsza ('alder tree') with the suffix -nica (glossed by Adamy as Stadt am Erlenbach, 'town on the alder stream'); Germanized as Oels.

b_przemkow.first_mention_attestation: 1280 AD (granted town rights by Duke Przemko of Ścinawa and named after him)
b_przemkow.eponym_details: Named after Duke Przemko of Ścinawa (c. 1255–1289), a Silesian Piast duke who granted the settlement town rights in 1280.
b_przemkow.etymology_analysis: Patronymic/possessive toponym from the personal name Przemko (diminutive of Przemysław), named after Duke Przemko of Ścinawa in 1280; Germanized as Primkenau.

b_wlen.first_mention_attestation: 1108 AD (castellany founded c. 1108 under Bolesław III Wrymouth; 1146 AD attested as 'Wlan' and 'Valan')
b_wlen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish wał ('rampart, earthen wall', reflected in 1146 Valan/Wlan), referring to the Piast border fortress; Germanized as Lähn.

b_swiny.first_mention_attestation: 1108 AD (first documented as 'oppidium Svini in Poloniae' in Cosmas of Prague's Chronica Boemorum)
b_swiny.etymology_analysis: Derived from Polish świnia ('swine, wild boar'), linked to a legend of knight Biwoy killing a wild boar; Germanized as Schweinhaus.

b_schweibus.etymology_analysis: German Schwiebus (Schweibus) is a phonetic adaptation of Polish Świebodzin, a possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Świeboda ('freedom, wealth') + -in.

b_siedlischo.first_mention_attestation: 1298 AD (castle of 'Sedlischo' / 'Sedlscho' first mentioned in a deed of Duke Henry III of Głogów)
b_siedlischo.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish siedlisko ('settlement, homestead'), attested in 1298 as Sedlischo/Sedlscho (later Carolath after 16th-c. Carolath Castle; Polish Siedlisko restored in 1946).

b_bytom.first_mention_attestation: 1005 AD (Slavic gród mentioned in 1005; famously defended against Henry V in 1109 as 'Bytom'/'Butum')
b_bytom.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish byt ('existence, dwelling place'), denoting a place of habitation/settlement; Germanized as Beuthen an der Oder (Niederbeuthen).

b_sprottau.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in 1000 AD in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg (meeting of Emperor Otto III and Bolesław I the Brave near Ilua/Iława, today a district of Szprotawa).
b_sprottau.etymology_analysis: German Sprottau is an adaptation of Polish Szprotawa, named after the Szprotawa River at whose confluence with the Bóbr the town lies. Nearby Iława (Ilua) is mentioned in 1000 AD by Thietmar of Merseburg.

b_zagan.first_mention_attestation: First historically attested on 23 May 1202 as a castellany seat (castellanus meus de Sagan) in a charter issued by Duke Henry I the Bearded for Lubiąż Abbey.

morphemes.translation: toponymic suffix denoting place of burnt/cleared forest

b_zagan.etymology_analysis: From Old Polish *żegać ('to burn'), referring to a settlement established on land cleared by slash-and-burn (place of the burnt forest). Legendary founding c. 700 AD by Princess Żaganna lacks contemporary attestation.

b_nowogrodziec.first_mention_attestation: Castle founded in 1202 by Duke Henry I the Bearded; town established and granted Magdeburg rights in 1233 (German: Naumburg am Queis).
b_nowogrodziec.etymology_analysis: Means 'new little stronghold' (calquing German Naumburg, 'new castle/borough' on the Kwisa River).

b_czersk.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned under the year 1142 in the Laurentian Codex as Чьрньскъ (Čьrnьsk); later spelled Cirnsk (1236–1237) and Cyrnsko (1242).
b_czersk.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby Czarna ('Black') River, a tributary of the Vistula, with the Slavic toponymic suffix -ъsko (Čьrnьsk -> Czyrńsko -> Czersk). Note: this is Czersk in Masovia (d_mazovia), not Czersk in Pomerania.

b_warszawa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records on 23 April 1313 in the ducal titulature of Siemowit II of Masovia (as Warszewa).
b_warszawa.eponym_details: Likely derived from the possessive form of the Old Polish personal name Warsz (shortened from Warcisław or Wrocisław), hypothesized to be a 13th-century nobleman of the Rawa clan who held a ducal grant on the site.
b_warszawa.etymology_analysis: Originally recorded as Warszewa / Warszowa ('belonging to Warsz'), shifting to Warszawa in the 15th–16th centuries via Masovian hypercorrection of -e- to -a-.

b_liw.first_mention_attestation: First written mention in 1304 in a ducal document of Bolesław II of Masovia, and again in 1335 under Siemowit III of Czersk.
b_liw.etymology_analysis: Closely linked to the Liwiec River (alternatively called Liw) guarding the eastern Masovian ford; etymologically connected to Slavic/Baltic roots for wet, boggy terrain.

b_brodno.first_mention_attestation: Although an archaeological stronghold existed in the 9th–10th centuries, the name Bródno was first recorded in written sources in 1414–1425.
b_brodno.etymology_analysis: Derived from the nearby Brodnia River and the Polish word bród ('ford'). An early medieval gord existed here in the 9th–10th centuries, but written attestation of the name dates to 1414–1425.

b_garwolin.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in medieval written notes in 1386 (and 1404); received its town charter in 1423.
b_garwolin.eponym_details: Derived from the medieval Old Polish personal name Garwoł (dates of the eponymous bearer unknown).
b_garwolin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Garwoł (folk etymology later connected it to gawrony, 'rooks').

b_gostynin.first_mention_attestation: Expanded around 1240 by Duke Konrad I of Masovia (burned in 1286; castellany by 1329). An archaeological Slavic gord existed nearby in the 6th–8th centuries.
b_gostynin.eponym_details: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Gostynia / Gościna (from gość 'guest').
b_gostynin.etymology_analysis: Possessive place name from the Old Polish personal name Gostynia; an early medieval gord stood nearby in the 6th–8th centuries, but historical records begin in the 13th century.

b_rawa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in historical sources in 1228 (and 1288); received town rights in 1321 (Latin: Rava oppidum).

morphemes.translation: from Rawka River / Proto-Slavic *rava ('slow/quiet water' or 'marshy stream')

b_rawa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Rawka (formerly Rawa) River on which the medieval gord was built.

b_sochaczew.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in documents from 1138, when Duke Bolesław III Wrymouth died at the local Benedictine monastery.

morphemes.translation: wooden ard/plough or dry forked tree branches

b_sochaczew.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish socha ('wooden plough' or 'forked branch/pole', or via personal name Sochacz).

b_lowicz.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Loviche in the Papal Bull of Gniezno issued by Pope Innocent II on 7 July 1136.
b_lowicz.eponym_details: Possibly from the Old Polish personal name Łowik (from łowić 'to hunt') or directly from a hunting ground.
b_lowicz.etymology_analysis: From Proto-Slavic *loviti ('to hunt'), either via personal name Łowik + possessive suffix -jь or directly denoting a hunting forest/settlement.

b_lomza.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century at Stara Łomża, but first mentioned in official written records in the 14th century (c. 1400; municipal rights in 1416/1418).
b_lomza.etymology_analysis: Scholarly consensus (Nazwy miejscowe Polski) points to a Baltic-influenced or hybrid Polish-Baltic hydronymic/topographic origin (Lithuanian loma 'low-lying wet meadow', or Polish łom + Baltic suffix -ża).

b_wizna.first_mention_attestation: Existence confirmed in written sources in 1145 (campaign of Grand Prince Vsevolod II of Kiev), and as a castellany in 1170.

morphemes.translation: uncertain root (possibly Baltic/hydronymic related to marsh/water)

b_wizna.etymology_analysis: Etymology is uncertain and debated; likely derived from a pre-Slavic/Baltic hydronymic or marshland root with the Slavic suffix -na.

b_kolno.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in written records in 1222 (or 1422 in Polish records; town charter in 1425). An 8th–9th century Lechitic stronghold existed at Stare Kolno.
b_kolno.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish *koł ('stake/palisade' or 'circle/enclosure') with the toponymic suffix -no.

b_plock.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 10th century (Benedictine abbey in 1009, diocese in 1075); first recorded in writing as urbs Plocensis / civitas Plocensis in Gallus Anonymus's chronicle (1112–1116).
b_plock.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from Old Polish płot ('palisade/fence') + -sk, or from a hydronym/topographic root *Płot-/*Płoc-.

b_wyszgorod.first_mention_attestation: First written mention dated to 1065 (Mogilno document); recorded as castellum Wysegrad by Gallus Anonymus (1112–1116).
b_wyszgorod.etymology_analysis: Compound Old Polish name meaning 'high stronghold' (Wysegrad -> Wyszogród), referring to its elevated position on Castle Hill above the Vistula.

b_zawkrze.first_mention_attestation: Granted Chełmno town rights in 1383 by Duke Siemowit IV of Masovia (early medieval stronghold on site dates to 9th–10th century).

morphemes.translation: from Szronka River / śreń ('thin ice / frost')

b_zawkrze.etymology_analysis: Named Szreńsk (in the historic region of Zawkrze) after the local Szronka River / Old Polish śreń ('crust of ice/frost') with suffix -sk.

b_ciechanow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in the 1065 Mogilno document of King Bolesław II the Bold as one of 19 grods (castrum) paying tithes to Mogilno Abbey.
b_ciechanow.eponym_details: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Ciechan (shortened from Ciechosław).
b_ciechanow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Ciechan ('belonging to Ciechan').

b_zakroczym.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned c. 1155 as a gord and settlement belonging to the Benedictine Monastery in Mogilno.
b_zakroczym.etymology_analysis: From Old Polish zakrot ('river crossing') or 'beyond Kroczym' (the older riverside settlement moved upslope due to Vistula floods).

b_nur.first_mention_attestation: Parish established probably in the 12th century; Land of Nur formally established in 1377 at a meeting of Masovian dukes in Sochaczew (town charter in 1410 or 1425).
b_nur.etymology_analysis: Originally a topographic term denoting wet, marshy ground along the Bug River.

b_wyszkow.first_mention_attestation: The village of Wyszków was first documented in 1203; granted town rights in 1502.
b_wyszkow.eponym_details: Possibly from the Old Polish personal name Wyszek / Wysz (from Wyszesław) or from wysok- ('high' escarpment above the Bug).
b_wyszkow.etymology_analysis: Likely possessive from the Old Polish personal name Wyszek/Wysz, or topographic from the high escarpment above the Bug River.

b_rozan.first_mention_attestation: Existed as a ducal village/gord (Rożan) in the 12th–13th centuries; received its town charter in 1378 from Duke Janusz I of Masovia.
b_rozan.etymology_analysis: Earlier form Rożan; derived either from róg ('horn/river bend' on the Narew) or rózga/róża.

b_bethen.first_mention_attestation: Originally recorded as Bitom in 1136 (Bull of Gniezno); archaeological gord dates to the early 11th century.
b_bethen.eponym_details: Possibly from an Old Polish personal name Bytom (shortened from a compound name in Byto-).
