b_bethen.etymology_analysis: German Beuthen (Bethen) is an adaptation of Polish Bytom, formed with the possessive suffix -jь from the Old Polish personal name Bytom.

b_lubliniec.first_mention_attestation: Established around 1270 by Duke Władysław of Opole (recorded as Lubie, Lublin, Lubin, later Lubliniec).
b_lubliniec.etymology_analysis: Derived from the root lub- ('pleasant/beloved', or personal name Lubla), with diminutive suffix -iniec to distinguish it from Lublin.

b_brzeg.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1234 as Visoke breg ('high bank') and in Latin as Civitas Altae Ripae; granted Magdeburg rights in 1248.
b_brzeg.etymology_analysis: Literally Polish brzeg ('bank, shore'), shortened from 1234 Visoke breg ('high bank' of the Oder, Latin Alta Ripa).

b_olawa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Latinized Old Polish form as Oleva in a papal document of Pope Innocent III on 12 August 1201.
b_olawa.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Oława River (German Ohlau), from the Indo-European/Slavic hydronymic root *ol-/*el- ('water').

b_otmunchow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Otemochow in 1155 (Bull of Adrian IV); also Othmuchow in the 13th-century Book of Henryków.
b_otmunchow.eponym_details: Derived from an Old Polish personal name *Otmuch (or *Otemoch).
b_otmunchow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Otmuch/Otemoch (Germanized as Ottmachau).

b_cieszyn.first_mention_attestation: First historically attested as Tescin in the Papal Bull of Adrian IV (1155). The 810 AD Three Brothers founding story is legendary.
b_cieszyn.eponym_details: Possessive from the Old Polish personal name Ciesza (shortened from Cieszymir/Cieszysław), or folk etymology from cieszym się ('we rejoice').
b_cieszyn.etymology_analysis: Possessive place name from Old Polish personal name Ciesza (German Teschen, Czech Těšín).

b_bielsko.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Belsko in a copy of a lost charter of Duke Mieszko I of Cieszyn (dated 1290–1310), and as zu Bilitz in 1312.

morphemes.translation: white / bleached podzol soil (gleby bielicowe) or marshy meadow (biel)

b_bielsko.etymology_analysis: Slavic toponym derived from biel ('podzol/whitish soil' or 'wet meadow') with the suffix -sko (Germanized as Bielitz).

b_nysa.first_mention_attestation: The river Nysa Kłodzka is attested as Niżą in 991 (Cosmas) and 1000 (Otto III); the town of Nysa itself is first attested in 1223 when granted Flemish town law.

morphemes.translation: low-flowing river or flowing stream (Nysa Kłodzka)

b_nysa.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Nysa Kłodzka River (German Neisse), an ancient Slavic/pre-Slavic hydronym attested from 991 AD.

b_glogowek.first_mention_attestation: First unequivocal historical mention in 1212 as Glogov in a tithing list of Lubiąż Abbey (an earlier 1076 attribution is a misidentification with Głogów).
b_glogowek.etymology_analysis: From Polish głóg ('hawthorn', abundant locally), with diminutive -ówek ('Little Głogów', German Oberglogau).

b_frankenstein.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the late 13th century (c. 1280) under Henry IV Probus; first mentioned as civitas Frankenstein on 10 January 1287.

morphemes.translation: stone/castle (from failed nearby town Löwenstein / Koziniec)

b_frankenstein.etymology_analysis: German portmanteau name combining Frankenberg and Löwenstein, two earlier failed settlements nearby (renamed Ząbkowice Śląskie in 1945).

b_opole.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 845 AD in the Bavarian Geographer (Descriptio civitatum et regionum ad septentrionalem plagam Danubii) as the tribe Opolini (20 civitates).

morphemes.translation: field / open country (medieval Slavic opole = territorial community of settlements)

b_opole.etymology_analysis: From the medieval West Slavic institution opole, denoting a territorial community/district of settlements centered on a stronghold.

b_kreuzburg.first_mention_attestation: Settlement built on 2 November 1252 by the Knights of the Cross with the Red Star as Cruceburg; received Magdeburg rights on 26 February 1253.

morphemes.translation: cross (referring to the Knights of the Cross with the Red Star)

b_kreuzburg.etymology_analysis: Named Cruceburg ('Cross-burgh', German Kreuzburg, Polonized as Kluczbork) by the Knights of the Cross with the Red Star who founded it in 1252.

b_strehlitz.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in 13th-century documents (c. 1235 / 1271) as a settlement and Piast ducal hunting center.
b_strehlitz.etymology_analysis: From Old Polish strzelec ('hunter/archer', plural strzelce), denoting a ducal service settlement of hunters (Germanized as Groß Strehlitz).

b_ratibor.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly mentioned by name as Ratibor in Gallus Anonymus's chronicle (1108 / 1112–1116). The 845 Bavarian Geographer mentions Golensizi (5 civitates) without naming Racibórz.
b_ratibor.eponym_details: Derived from the Slavic personal name Racibor (Proto-Slavic *Ratiborъ, 'war-fighter').
b_ratibor.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Slavic personal name Racibor (Czech Ratiboř, German Ratibor).

b_rybnik.first_mention_attestation: Origins trace to 9th–10th century Slavic settlements; first written mentions appear around the late 12th–13th century (town charter before 1308).
b_rybnik.etymology_analysis: Old Polish rybnik means 'fishpond', reflecting medieval fish farming in the settlement.

b_gniezno.first_mention_attestation: First written mention as Schinesghe in the Dagome iudex (c. 991), and as Gnesin urbs / Gnesen in Thietmar of Merseburg (1012–1018). Stronghold founded just before 940.
b_gniezno.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to Old Polish gniazdo ('nest', per Gallus Anonymus and the Lech legend); alternative hypotheses link it to a vanished Lake Gniezno or Slavic kniaź ('prince').

b_sroda.first_mention_attestation: Oldest known written mention dates to 1228 (and as Sroda in a 1281 charter of Przemysł II).

morphemes.translation: Wednesday (middle day of the week, when markets were held)

b_sroda.etymology_analysis: Named after Wednesday (Old Polish śrzoda), the market day of the medieval settlement.

b_pyzdry.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1232 during Duke Henry I the Bearded's campaign in Greater Poland.

morphemes.translation: obscure root (possibly linked to puch/pyzdr- 'swollen/elevated bank' or personal name)

b_pyzdry.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greater Polish toponym first attested in 1232; exact lexical root is debated.

b_konin.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in written documents in 1250 (Lisiec ante Conin) and 1283 (civitas nostra Kunyn).
b_konin.eponym_details: Derived from the zoonymic Old Polish personal name Koń ('horse').
b_konin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Koń ('horse', also depicted on the town's coat of arms).

b_kalisz.first_mention_attestation: Identified by many historians with Calisia (Καλισία), mentioned c. 158 AD by Claudius Ptolemy in his Geography (though some scholars dispute the identification; first medieval mention is Kalis in Gallus Anonymus, 1112–1116, for 1106).
b_kalisz.etymology_analysis: Derived from the archaic Slavic root kal ('swamp/marsh'), referring to the marshy Prosna River valley.

b_kozmin.first_mention_attestation: Oldest known mention comes from 1232 as a village owned by the Knights Templar (Cosmin opido Polonie c. 1300).
b_kozmin.eponym_details: Likely from the Old Polish personal name Koźma (Cosmas) or kozieł ('goat').
b_kozmin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Koźma (until 1997 officially named Koźmin).

b_turek.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Turcoviste in the Papal Bull of Gniezno issued by Pope Innocent II in 1136 as a possession of the Archbishops of Gniezno.
b_turek.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish tur ('aurochs', early form Turcoviste 'place of aurochs').

b_naklo.first_mention_attestation: Developed as a Pomeranian settlement by the mid-10th century; first mentioned in 11th/early 12th-century documents (captured by Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1109–1113; Gallus Anonymus).
b_naklo.etymology_analysis: Originally Nakieł (morphed to Nakło in the 16th century), from Old Polish nakieł denoting a wet, boggy riverside site or bend on the Noteć River.

b_zlotow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1370 in the chronicle of Jan of Czarnków (and granted Magdeburg rights in 1370). An 8th-century Slavic settlement existed archaeologically.
b_zlotow.eponym_details: Likely from the Old Polish personal name Złoty ('golden') or from złoto ('gold').
b_zlotow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from Old Polish Złoty / złoto ('gold'; German Flatow).

b_znin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as provincia de Znein cum foro in the Papal Bull of Gniezno on 7 July 1136.
b_znin.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish żnieja ('harvest/harvester'); an early medieval gord existed nearby in the 6th–8th centuries, with written attestation beginning in 1136.

b_lebus.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Liubusua and Libusua urbs in Thietmar of Merseburg's chronicle (1012–1018). The Slavic Leubuzzi tribe inhabited the area from c. 7th century.
b_lebus.etymology_analysis: West Slavic stronghold name Liubusua (Polish Lubusz, German Lebus), associated with the Leubuzzi tribe and Proto-Slavic *ljubъ ('dear/pleasant').

b_oderfrankfurt.first_mention_attestation: The West Slavic trading settlement of Zliwitz (Zbiwitz / Zliwiz) on the Oder was granted staple rights by Duke Henry I the Bearded in 1225; chartered as Vrankenvorde (Frankfurt) in 1253.

morphemes.translation: obscure root (possibly plum/śliwa or distorted Zbiwitz)

b_oderfrankfurt.etymology_analysis: Zliwitz (Zliwiz, Zbiwitz) was the pre-1253 West Slavic settlement on the Oder; Polish Wikipedia notes its original form and meaning are unclear due to scribal distortion. In 1253 it was chartered as Vrankenvorde (Frankfurt an der Oder).

b_sulecin.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in documents in 1241 (and 1244 as Zulenche), when Henry I the Bearded / Bishop Henry granted it to Mroczko of Pogorzela.
b_sulecin.eponym_details: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Sulęta (shortened from Sulimir or Sulisław).
b_sulecin.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Sulęta (Germanized as Zielenzig).

b_rzepin.first_mention_attestation: Founded on the site of a 10th-century fort; first documented in the late 13th century (German Reppen, 1297/1329).
b_rzepin.eponym_details: Derived from Old Polish Rzepa ('turnip') or a personal nickname Rzepa.
b_rzepin.etymology_analysis: Slavic toponym derived from rzepa ('turnip') or the personal nickname Rzepa (Germanized as Reppen).

b_poznan.first_mention_attestation: Earliest known written reference is in Thietmar of Merseburg's chronicle for the year 970 (episcopus Posnaniensis, 'bishop of Poznań') and 1005 (ab urbe Posnani).
b_poznan.eponym_details: Possibly from an Old Polish personal name *Poznan (participle of poznać 'to know/recognize').

morphemes.translation: known/recognized (from poznać 'to meet/know', or personal name Poznan)

b_poznan.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Poznan (or verb poznać 'to know/meet'), denoting 'Poznan's stronghold' or a meeting place.

b_miedzyrzecz.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1005 as Mezerici by Thietmar of Merseburg during King Henry II's campaign against Bolesław I the Brave; later Mezyriecze in Gallus Anonymus (1112–1116).
b_miedzyrzecz.etymology_analysis: Topographic settlement name meaning '(place) between the rivers', referring to its location at the confluence of the Obra and Paklica rivers.

b_czarnkow.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned as Carnkou / Charncou for 1108 in Gallus Anonymus's Gesta principum Polonorum (1112–1116) when reconquered by Bolesław III Wrymouth.
b_czarnkow.eponym_details: Derived from the Old Polish personal name Czarnek ('black/dark one').
b_czarnkow.etymology_analysis: Possessive toponym from the Old Polish personal name Czarnek ('belonging to Czarnek').

b_wronki.first_mention_attestation: Oldest known written mention dates to 1279.
b_wronki.etymology_analysis: Derived from Polish wrona ('crow'), reflected in the town's coat of arms.

b_wolsztyn.first_mention_attestation: Established around 1285 on a causeway across the Dojca River, probably by Cistercian monks from Obra Abbey (first area documents from mid-12th century).
b_wolsztyn.etymology_analysis: Polonization of German Wollstein ('wool-stone/town'), reflecting the medieval wool and cloth trade of the Cistercian-founded settlement.

b_wschowa.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1290 as Frovenstat (Fraustadt) in a charter of Duke Henry of Głogów, and as Weschowam in the Liber fundationis episcopatus Vratislaviensis (1295–1305).
b_wschowa.eponym_details: Alternatively derived from Old Polish personal name Wiesz (shortened from Wielisław), or from wschować ('to shelter/hide').
b_wschowa.etymology_analysis: Either possessive from Old Polish personal name Wiesz (Veschov) or from Old Polish wschować ('place of refuge/shelter'). German Fraustadt (1290 Frovenstat) refers to the Virgin Mary.

b_koscian.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in written sources in 1242 in the form Costan.
b_koscian.eponym_details: Possibly from an Old Polish personal name Kościan/Kościen, or from a wetland plant name.

morphemes.translation: sharp reed/sedge (koszczka) or personal name Kościan

b_koscian.etymology_analysis: Derived from Old Polish kościan/koścień ('sharp reed/bulrush' growing in the Obra marshes) or from the personal name Kościan.

b_srem.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in writing as Zrem in the Papal Bull of Gniezno (1136); archaeological stronghold dates to the second half of the 10th century.
b_srem.eponym_details: Possibly from an Old Polish personal name *Śrzem / *Srem.

morphemes.translation: obscure root (possibly related to *sermъ 'stream/current' or personal name)

b_srem.etymology_analysis: Old Polish toponym attested from 1136 (Zrem), likely from an archaic Slavic root or personal name.
